approachQuestion.prompt:
Rescue capsules

A sorted array w gives positive passenger weights. Each capsule holds at most two passengers and total weight at most L. Every passenger must travel in exactly one capsule; all passengers individually weigh at most L. Return the minimum capsule count.

Example 1: w=[1,2,2,3], L=4 → 2, pairing 1 with 3 and 2 with 2.
Example 2: w=[2,3,3], L=4 → 3.
Example 3: w=[] → 0.

Constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 200000; 1 ≤ w[i] ≤ L ≤ 10^9; w is already nondecreasing. Input is read-only. Return only the stated scalar result. All arithmetic and comparisons use constant-time exact 64-bit operations; all intermediate values fit.

options.text: Maintain lightest and heaviest remaining indices. Allocate one capsule for the heaviest. If a distinct lightest passenger fits beside them, consume that passenger too. Always consume the heaviest and continue until no passengers remain.
options.feedback: If the lightest cannot pair with the heaviest, nobody can, so the heaviest must go alone. If they can pair, an optimal arrangement can be exchanged to pair them: if both had other partners, those partners can pair because one was paired with the heaviest and the other is no heavier than the heaviest. This does not increase capsule count.

options.text: Pair adjacent passengers from the lightest end whenever they fit, otherwise send the lightest alone.
options.feedback: Small-small pairing can strand two large passengers. For [1,2,2,3] and L=4, this uses three capsules instead of two.

options.text: Return the ceiling of total weight divided by L.
options.feedback: Weight capacity is not the only constraint: each capsule holds at most two passengers. For [1,1,1] and L=10, this gives one but two capsules are required.

options.text: Enumerate every legal sequence of decisions, evaluate each complete candidate, and return the best result.
options.feedback: Exhaustive search can find the right result, but revisits combinations of decisions that the safe local rule resolves directly. The number of candidates grows far beyond what the input limit permits.

details: Maintain lightest and heaviest remaining indices. Allocate one capsule for the heaviest. If a distinct lightest passenger fits beside them, consume that passenger too. Always consume the heaviest and continue until no passengers remain.

The heaviest remaining passenger needs a capsule. If even the lightest cannot share it, nobody can; otherwise pairing them preserves capacity for the rest. The at-most-two-passengers rule is essential to this exchange argument.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed frontier method, regardless of your previous choice. Use exactly the frontier method above as iterative scans with scalar indices, counters and accumulators. Do not copy the input and do not store a decision list. Let n be the number of input records or positions. Choose the tightest standard worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Input and returned scalar are excluded. All other live storage, including copying and any call stack, is counted. No hashing or expected-time operations are used.

feedback.reason: Each capsule consumes the heaviest endpoint and optionally the lightest.

messages.text: The method stores no per-item history or copied input.
The scans do not restart for each item.
In the worst case every input item can affect the answer.

details: Every capsule consumes the heaviest remaining passenger, and may also consume the lightest. At most n iterations therefore handle all passengers. The two indices and capsule count are O(1) auxiliary storage.
“Time O(n), auxiliary space O(n)”: The method stores no per-item history or copied input.
“Time O(n²), auxiliary space O(1)”: The scans do not restart for each item.
“Time O(1), auxiliary space O(1)”: In the worst case every input item can affect the answer.
